passages.original: Hippocrates et Epicydes non tam tutum prima specie quam unum spe undique abscisa consilium esse rati, ut se militibus permitterent et adsuetis magna ex parte sibi et tum fama caedis commilitonum accensis, obuiam agmini procedunt. prima forte signa sescentorum Cretensium erant, qui apud Hieronymum meruerant sub eis et Hannibalis beneficium habebant, capti ad Trasumennum inter Romanorum auxilia dimissique. quos ubi ex signis armorumque habitu cognouere Hippocrates atque Epicydes, ramos oleae ac uelamenta alia supplicum porrigentes orare ut reciperent sese, receptos tutarentur neu proderent Syracusanis, a quibus ipsi mox trucidandi populo Romano dederentur.
passages.english: Hippocrates and Epicydes, judging that the one course left to them, now that hope was cut off on every side, was not so much safe at first sight as the only one, namely to entrust themselves to the soldiers, who were for the most part accustomed to them and were at that moment inflamed by the report of the slaughter of their fellow soldiers, went out to meet the column. As it happened, the leading standards were those of six hundred Cretans, who had served under them in Hieronymus' time and were under an obligation to Hannibal for a kindness, having been captured at Trasimene among the auxiliaries of the Romans and released. When Hippocrates and Epicydes recognized them from their standards and the style of their arms, they held out olive branches and the other coverings of suppliants and begged them to take them in, to protect them once taken in, and not to betray them to the Syracusans, by whom they themselves would soon be handed over to the Roman people to be butchered.
passages.notes: "velamenta" are the wool-wreathed coverings (fillets) carried by suppliants. "Hannibalis beneficium habebant": literally "had a kindness from Hannibal", i.e. owed him gratitude for their release.
